Use “bevor” (before) and tell it apart from “vor” (preposition) and “vorher” (adverb).
Use “seitdem / seit” for something that began in the past and is still going on.

It's May 2030. Friedrich has kept his promise: he's invited Grete to Lübeck. Mara and Jakob are going with her, by train. Mrs Hoffmann is sitting at the window, in her wheelchair.
How are you feeling? Before we left, you were so pale.
I was nervous, child. I haven't travelled by train for forty years. Since I got old, I've only been on the stairs. And even those only on a chair.
Would you like something to drink while we wait? We have to change trains in Hamburg.
A tea would be nice. And, Jakob, let me know as soon as we see the sea. I don't want to miss the first moment.
We won't see the sea until Travemünde. That's another two hours.
Two hours. I've waited sixty-five years. I can manage two more hours.
Did you often go to the Baltic Sea in the old days?

When I was a child, every year, before the war started. With my parents, to Warnemünde. My father used to carry me into the water on his shoulders, until the waves got too big. And later, while I was studying, once with Friedrich. In the summer of 1960. We slept on the beach, in a wicker beach chair, until the seagulls woke us.
It was wonderful. And as long as I live, I'll remember it. But now, child, please wake me before we get to Hamburg. I'd like to sleep a little while the train is moving. Like back then.
“SHTRAHNT-korp”: final d and b are devoiced.
Wir fahren morgen. Vorher packen wir.
The same logic applies to “nach”: nachdem (conjunction), nach (preposition), danach / nachher (adverb).
“während” = while (two actions at the same time). Careful: “während” is also a preposition with the genitive (chapter 29):
While she was sleeping, the train kept going. (conjunction)
During the journey she slept. (preposition + genitive)
“seitdem / seit” = since (the action began in the past and is still going on). Usually with the PRESENT in the main clause:
Since I've been living in Berlin, I've taken the tram.

As with the preposition “seit” (seit drei Jahren), German uses the PRESENT for what is still going on: “Ich wohne seit drei Jahren hier” (not “habe gewohnt”). English uses the present perfect here: “I've lived here for three years.”
Wir bleiben, bis die Sonne untergeht.
Sobald wir ankommen, rufe ich dich an.
Solange ich lebe, werde ich mich daran erinnern.
After “sobald” and “nachdem”, the action in the subordinate clause ends before the one in the main clause: “Sobald ich gegessen habe, gehe ich.”
They are all subordinating conjunctions: the conjugated verb goes to the END. If the subordinate clause comes first, the main clause starts with the verb.
While she was sleeping, the train kept going.
Since she saw Friedrich again, she's been playing every day.
As long as I live, I'll remember.

Since I've had a dog, I walk more.
As soon as I have time, I'll visit you.

Before they left, Mara had spent three days planning everything. The train had been booked, with a space for the wheelchair. A suitcase had been packed, with warm jumpers, because Mrs Hoffmann said it could be cold on the Baltic even in May. Dr Yılmaz had examined Mrs Hoffmann and said the journey wasn't a problem, as long as she didn't overexert herself. Mrs Hoffmann had replied: “For ninety-three years I haven't overexerted myself. Now it's time.” Dr Yılmaz had laughed and given her a prescription for heart pills.

The journey took four hours. While Mrs Hoffmann slept, Mara and Jakob looked out of the window at the flat green fields, the yellow rapeseed fields, the red-brick churches in the small villages. Jakob was holding Mara's hand. They had had many moments like this in recent months, quiet ones, without big words. Since they had met in the autumn, not a day had gone by without them talking to each other.

In Lübeck, Friedrich was waiting at the station, also in a wheelchair, pushed by Sophie. He was holding a single red rose, and when the train stopped and Mrs Hoffmann was lifted out of the carriage, he raised the rose like a tram driver giving a signal. The two wheelchairs stood side by side on the platform, and the two old people looked at each other and laughed, because it was so absurd and so beautiful.
Two old sets of wheels on a platform. Who would have thought it in 1961, Grete?
Not me. I thought I'd never see you again. But I always hoped. Until today.

On the first day, Friedrich showed them Lübeck's old town, which lies on an island between two rivers. The Holstentor with its two thick round towers, the old crooked merchants' houses, the narrow passages between the courtyards. They ate marzipan in an old café where marzipan has been made for two hundred years. Mrs Hoffmann ate three pieces. “Since I've been playing the piano again, I've been hungry again,” she said. Friedrich said that in Lübeck you can't put on weight as long as you play Brahms every day.

In the evening they were invited to Friedrich's house on the banks of the Trave, an old, narrow house with green shutters, right by the water. On the ground floor there was a music room with a black piano, shelves full of sheet music and a window through which you could see the boats on the river. On the piano there was a small black-and-white photo in a silver frame. Mrs Hoffmann saw it and held her breath. It was herself, at twenty-four, on the beach at Warnemünde, in the summer of 1960, with her hair in the wind and a laugh she hadn't seen for decades. “That has always stood here,” Friedrich said quietly. “Even when my wife was still alive. She knew who it was. She said: everyone has a piece of music they mustn't forget. This was yours.” Grete said nothing. But that night she played Friedrich's piano until the stars came out over the Trave, and Friedrich sat beside her and listened, with his eyes closed.

On the second day they went to Travemünde, to the sea. Sophie had organised a big taxi. It was a clear, cool May day, the sky was light blue, and the wind smelt of salt. When the taxi went over the last dune and the sea suddenly appeared in front of them, grey, blue and silver, endless all the way to the horizon, Jakob said quietly: “Mrs Hoffmann. The sea.” As he had promised. As soon as they saw it.

Mrs Hoffmann said nothing for a long time. She just looked. Her eyes, those lively blue eyes Mara had seen on her first day on the fourth floor, filled with tears. Then she said, so quietly that only Mara heard: “My father carried me here on his shoulders. Before the war came. Before everything came.”

They pushed the two wheelchairs along a wooden path right up close to the water, where the sand was firm. Sophie had hired two wicker beach chairs, but Grete and Friedrich didn't want to sit in them. They wanted to sit side by side, hand in hand, and watch the waves, as they had seventy years ago. The seagulls were screeching above them. Children were building sandcastles. A dog ran into the water and back and shook itself right next to Friedrich, who laughed until he had to cough.

Mara and Jakob walked a little way along the beach, to leave the two of them alone. The water was icy, but Mara took off her shoes anyway and walked barefoot through the waves. It was the first time she had seen the Baltic Sea. It was different from the Black Sea of her childhood, colder, greyer, calmer. But the roar was the same.
Mara. Before we go back… I wanted to ask you something. I've thought about it a lot. Ever since I've known you, I've been wondering how long I should wait.
Mara stopped. The waves washed over her feet. Her heart was beating so hard that she could barely hear the sea.

My flat on Oderberger Straße becomes free in the summer. And on the second floor on Kastanienallee, next to the Nowaks, someone is moving out in August. I've talked to the landlord. To Ludwig. He says he'll only let it to someone you recommend to him.

Mara laughed, with wet feet and tears in her eyes. “You want to move into our house?” Jakob nodded. “Until we find a bigger flat,” he said. “Together. If you want.” Mara looked at the sea, then at Jakob, then back at the two wheelchairs in the distance, where two old people who had waited sixty-five years too long were sitting hand in hand. “Yes,” she said. “I do. And I don't want to wait as long as they did.”

They stayed on the beach until the sun set. The sky turned orange, then pink, then purple. Friedrich had brought his violin, and when the sun touched the water, he played, softly and gently, in his wheelchair, with the bow that had waited sixty-five years. Grete hummed along. A few passers-by stopped and listened. Nobody clapped. It was too beautiful to clap.

The next morning, at breakfast in Friedrich's kitchen, Mrs Hoffmann said she didn't want to go back to Berlin yet. “Just two weeks,” she said. “Until the lime trees are in blossom. Sophie said the guest room is free.” Mara looked at Friedrich. He looked like a young man who had just been given a present. So Mara and Jakob went back to Berlin alone, two days later, and held hands the whole way, while the yellow rapeseed fields went by outside.
